items.title: Diesel of Discontent
items.content:
“There are three things in the world that deserve no mercy: hypocrisy, fraud, and tyranny.” – Frederick William Robertson
 During the first six months of 2026, European buyers gorged on practically every liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo Russia’s Yamal plant could produce. Of the 140 ships that set sail from that facility, 136 offloaded their life-nourishing bounty in Europe, with France, Belgium, Spain, and the Netherlands quietly absorbing the bulk. Analysts estimate the revenue generated from these sales to be on the order of $7 billion—funds that were presumably funneled to President Vladimir Putin’s war machine, which is either on the brink of total collapse or fixing to march all the way to Paris, depending on which side of their mouths European leaders are lecturing from today.
 In May, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer—suffocating on terrible poll numbers and staring down the barrel of a diesel and jet fuel crisis of his own—enraged London’s spreadsheet dwellers by daring to carve out a sanctions exception allowing imports of Russian crude refined in India. Despite the firestorm, the exception remains, and a full accounting of just how much shadow diesel has made its way to His Majesty’s islands is unlikely to adorn the front pages of the Financial Times anytime soon.
 In perusing the hyperbolic coverage that has followed US President Donald Trump’s now-infamous dirty diesel deal with Putin, we find little acknowledgment of these glaring bits of hypocrisy. Take this missive from Politico , which sought commentary from various European Union leaders en route to whatever meaningless talking session they might have been attending on Monday morning:
 “ On their way into their meeting, the EU’s foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward. 
 ‘Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,’ Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said. 
 The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was ‘not planning to follow suit with’ purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up ‘economic pressure’ on Moscow. ”

 In her natural habitat | Getty 
 None of this is to excuse how Trump put himself in this position, of course. His failure to end the war in Ukraine swiftly upon taking office and the disastrous decision to go to war with Iran have compounded error upon error, and there is a direct line between these broken campaign promises and the electoral pickle in which he currently finds himself. His half-hearted return to his correct instinct that high energy prices make for bad politics might be a classic example of too little, too late, but late is still undefeated in the battle against never.

 Regrettable circumstances | Getty 
 As we have been arguing since April of 2022, the West’s entire approach to economic war against Putin’s Russia was fatally flawed from the start, doomed to the predictable loop of failures being experienced now. There is a better way, one that would breathe much-needed economic air into an anemic European economy, raise global standards of living from their current downward trajectory, and substantially ramp up real economic pressure against Redmanbad in Moscow. Let’s revisit the details.

items.title: Jump Ball
items.content:
“He hits from both sides of the plate. He’s amphibious.” – Yogi Berra
 On January 6, 2025, Indonesia formally acceded to full membership in BRICS, the starts-and-stops, Russia- and China-led organization seeking to create an alternative to the US dollar-based global financial system. As the war in Iran has since made clear, whatever limitations might be plaguing America’s wildly overfunded and corrupt military-industrial complex, its economic power and broad array of financial tools are still formidable. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s economic siege has arguably been more devastating to Iran than the best efforts of Pete Hegseth’s Department of War. Through this lens, the battles over BRICS and US dollar hegemony are not just side skirmishes of World War III, but pivotal and potentially decisive confrontations.
 Less than a year after Indonesia’s BRICS acceptance, student-led protests engulfed the island nation—a dubious coincidence. The campaign had many hallmarks of previous so-called color revolutions observed in former Soviet republics and other parts of the world, something Indonesian leaders seemed content to use as justification for their subsequent crackdown. Western think tanks were quick to call foul on that framing:
 “ Since late August, Indonesians have been protesting against police violence and politicians’ perks. Moscow and Beijing have taken advantage of this chaos, claiming it is a direct result of the United States meddling in the domestic affairs of an Asian nation. The Indonesian government and its diplomatic partners, as well as the public, should be aware of these operations. Moreover, governments and intelligence experts should forecast the next steps Russia-China collaboration [sic] to enable preventative measures. 
 It is not new for Russia and China to frame demonstrations as Western-engineered: they have done so in response to domestic protests in Moscow and Hong Kong. The two countries have also discredited democracy protests elsewhere—including in Ukraine, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Serbia and Thailand—using claims of covert US interference in domestic politics. ”

 Organic or orchestrated? | Getty 
 Its accession to BRICS aside, Indonesia’s leaders have broadly tried to stay neutral in the battle between the geopolitical elephants, pursuing a strategy of strategic ambiguity. As with BRICS members India and Brazil, trade with China has created meaningful ties to that emerging superpower that would be nearly impossible to sever, yet the country still maintains significant interactions to the US military:
 “ Indonesia and the United States recently elevated their decades-long military ties to a Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP), a designation that embodies the countries’ commitment to pursue advanced security measures. 
 Under the MDCP, the nations will codevelop sophisticated asymmetric capabilities and other next-generation defense technologies across domains, and cooperate on maintenance, repair and overhaul support to ensure readiness, according to a joint statement released after Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., in April 2026. ”

 A little bit for everybody | Department of War 
 At first blush, neutrality between superpowers would seem a near-impossible task, especially given Indonesia’s role as a gatekeeper of the Strait of Malacca, a global shipping chokepoint on par with the Strait of Hormuz in its economic significance. Surely, the country will soon be forced to firmly and decisively choose a side and cast its lot with either Washington or the Beijing-Moscow axis. Or will it? Let’s explore the strategic implications.

items.title: Ties That Bind
items.content:
“No nation was ever ruined by trade.” – Benjamin Franklin
 With a land area equal to that of Arizona and a population of just 27,000, Labrador—the onshore portion of the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL)—is one of the most resource-rich yet largely undeveloped regions in the Western Hemisphere. Abundant timber, iron ore, nickel, copper, cobalt, gold, rare earths, and other critical mineral prospects dot its rural landscape, and its large rivers provide enormous hydroelectric potential. Think of it as an even more thinly populated version of Alaska.

 Don’t pretend like you knew where it was | Wiki Commons 
 The border separating Labrador from Québec was not officially decided until March 1, 1927, when the Judicial Committee of the British Privy Council ruled largely in favour of what was then the Dominion of Newfoundland in its boundary dispute with Canada (NL would not join Canada as a province until 1949). The border, which Québec governments still do not formally recognize, largely follows the height of the land separating rivers that drain east to the Atlantic from those draining west and north toward Hudson Bay and the Arctic.
 By far the largest hydroelectric power facility in Labrador is the Churchill Falls Generating Station on the Churchill River. Its 11 turbines combine for a nameplate capacity of 5.4 gigawatts (GW), vastly more electricity than local residents currently consume. Under a contract signed in 1969 and not set to expire until 2041, the substantial majority of Churchill Falls’ output is sold to Hydro-Québec for the paltry sum of 0.2 Canadian cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh). Among the beneficiaries of this arrangement are Hydro-Québec’s many customers in the US Northeast, whose solar and wind installations rely upon the dispatchability afforded by the impoundment dams to their north.

 Practically free | Reuters 
 Understandably, the one-sided nature of this contract does not sit well with NL residents, and there have been several attempts to rebalance it over the years. The closest the two sides came to a new deal was a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in December of 2024 , but politics impeded its implementation as a binding agreement, and it expired in April of 2026. Enter newly elected Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who hopes to resolve the tensions between the two provinces by vastly expanding the pie to be split, providing cover for renegotiating this notoriously bad deal:
 “ The Carney government is pumping C$10 billion in federal backing into a massive hydroelectric project in Newfoundland and Labrador, pitching the project as part of its effort to strengthen Canada’s economy against President Donald Trump’s trade threats. 
 The federal support will help to advance a broader C$70 billion project to upgrade the Churchill Falls generating station and develop Gull Island. Prime Minister Mark Carney said it will be the largest clean energy project in North America, one that could eventually generate enough electricity to light up the equivalent of Canada’s three largest cities. ”
 The Churchill Falls announcement is just one in a flurry of generationally significant energy and mineral development projects that Carney has thrown the full weight of his Liberal government behind—much to the shock of those on Canada’s political left and right alike. His transformation has been so abrupt, and has unfolded at such speed, that critics remain convinced that none of it will come to pass. Assessing the situation more broadly, however, reveals a deeper agenda that, if real, could finally unlock the sleeping giant of Canada’s gargantuan natural endowment, extracting wealth on a scale few can fathom. Let’s head north and explore the source of our optimism.

items.title: Straw Clutching
items.content:
“Virtue is more to be feared than vice, because its excesses are not subject to the regulation of conscience.” - Adam Smith
 A classic trick in debate is distorting your opponent’s position, then nullifying your reframing of their view. This straw man tactic is particularly effective when the semantic maneuvering is sly and subtle, hence its permeation throughout political discourse.
 Consider the diesel crisis facing US President Donald Trump as he hurtles toward an ominous midterm election. Trump has many levers with which to restrain runaway domestic prices for that all-important fuel, and we have always been careful in our explanation of them. “Toggle” and “limit” are among the verbs we have chosen to describe his options on exports, for example. We have purposefully avoided the word “ban,” as such a drastic measure would unleash unintended consequences, including, possibly, making the problem worse.

 Up against it | Getty 
 There’s no room for subtlety when the cash register is ringing, and our friends in industry can be forgiven for wanting the party to continue just a bit longer. To that end, a powerful set of lobbyists and allies has worked to frame Trump’s choice as binary, either “ban” or “as you were,” and an avalanche of criticism has thundered through the media to nullify the former. Here’s an example editorial from The Wall Street Journal :
 “ Faced with record high diesel prices, some lawmakers are calling for a ban on US diesel exports. The argument sounds simple: If diesel is scarce, stop sending American-made fuel overseas and build up the supply at home. That misidentifies the problem… 
 …the diesel shortage isn’t a result of the US exporting too much fuel. It is a global refining crisis. US refiners are supplying American consumers while cushioning a volatile global market that is driving prices higher at home. ”
 The fallacious implication, of course, is that US refiners have an inherent right—nay, an obligation—to participate in said global markets. For all the lip service paid to the ideal of free-market capitalism, every refinery in the world operates with the express consent of the government where the asset resides, including in America. That consent is always conditional, and the US government is currently led by President Trump.
 That we were not the only ones aware of the game being played became clear last week, when industry veteran and current US Energy Secretary Chris Wright began spreading what amounted to a you-can-still-do-it-the-easy-way message :
 “ US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has contacted executives at several major American refiners in recent days to gauge support for a voluntary restriction on diesel exports as the Trump administration searches for ​an alternative to a short-term ban, according to three people familiar with the discussions. 
 The effort to enlist companies voluntarily underscores the limited options available to the White ‌House amid surging fuel prices that are pushing inflation higher and beginning to ripple through the broader economy as crucial November midterm elections approach. ”

 An offer you shouldn’t refuse | Getty 
 Having observed many such tussles between industry and Washington over the decades, we put pen to paper today to argue that the “limited options available” framing is little more than wishcasting on the part of those with a vested financial interest in elevated diesel prices. Like it or lump it, Trump has many cards to play to get his way ahead of the elections, and if he doesn’t succeed, life looks likely to get rather complicated for an industry currently riding high. It would be value-maximizing for industry players to play ball with him. Let’s explore why.

items.title: Going With the Flow
items.content:
“You’re running to be prime minister — it’s hard to be the person who makes jokes.” – Ed Miliband 
 Several months ago, we took to these pages to articulate an admittedly long-shot call. After foreseeing Mark Carney’s 180-degree flip on all things climate change, we postulated that perhaps Great Britain, Canada’s historical mothership, might also be ready to discard the geopolitical deadweight of carbon insanity. While searching for a British Carney—a politician with green bona fides so unquestioned as to put him above reproach in executing such a change—we settled on Ed Miliband. Thus followed our prediction that he might replace Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister. 
 If you are going to be wrong, you might as well be spectacularly so. Not only was Miliband shuffled off to the post of foreign secretary, but his successor as energy security and net zero secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, seems no less a climate warrior than he. For our many beleaguered subscribers in the United Kingdom (UK), we sincerely wish your government had more to offer you in the face of the greatest energy crisis of the modern era than this : 
 “ National Gas has moved into the advanced engineering design phase for a 350-mile hydrogen pipeline linking St Fergus in northeast Scotland to Teesside on England’s east coast, the gas transmission system operator said in a statement Sept. 17. 
 The pipeline is the second phase of Project Union, and National Gas plans to develop a 1,500-mile national hydrogen network connecting major industrial clusters and hydrogen production centers, the company said. 
 A first phase will connect Teesside, through Yorkshire and the Humber, and south into the East Midlands, through a 300-mile pipeline. ” 

 Can’t win ‘em all | Getty 
 While the rest of the world is busy reacting to a triple shortage of liquefied natural gas (LNG), crude oil, and refined products, His Majesty’s Royal Government is fixing to build a pipeline network for a molecule that nobody will produce because it is too expensive, in order to move it across vast distances despite nobody demanding that it be done, only for it to arrive at a location where nobody will have built the necessary-but-money-losing assets to make any use of it. And one wonders why the whiff of revolution is spreading across Britannia. 
 Since the onset of the war in Iran, we have been flagging how the European Union (EU) was both particularly vulnerable to a winter energy shock and—inexplicably—doing precious little to avert it. The Miliband-for-Fahnbulleh trade inspired us to take a narrower look at the energy predicament of its only defector (to date). Amazingly, the UK approaches the coldest months of the year in measurably worse condition, particularly susceptible to the whims of the very global leaders its population claims to detest. The numbers are downright scary, so let’s take a cautious peek.

items.title: Escalation Clauses
items.content:
“I think gas prices are a conspiracy.” – Tom Braidwood 
 On Sunday, a world chronically short of diesel woke up to the happy news that Ukraine—undoubtedly with the full support of those who currently occupy positions of power across Europe and Great Britain, and perhaps even the US—had caused significant damage at the Gazpromneft Moscow Refinery, a facility capable of handling 245,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil. In the weeks leading up to the Moscow attack, the Ryazan Oil Refinery (320,000 bpd), Saratov Refinery (140,000 bpd), Syzran Refinery (150,000 bpd), and Yaroslavl Refinery (300,000 bpd) were also hit, while reports circulated on Monday morning that Ukrainian drones had attacked the Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim Oil Refinery (190,000 bpd) as well. We are undoubtedly missing others. 

 Much rejoicing | AP 
 In unrelated news, voters in Germany expressed a certain amount of dissatisfaction with the country’s direction of travel, dealing a wildly embarrassing blow to its hapless chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Despite solidifying his place as the most unpopular leader in modern German history, Merz intends to keep pretending he has a mandate to lead, at least for now: 
 “ German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Sunday vowed to stay in office to press ahead with reforms despite heavy losses for his Christian Democratic Union party and a surge in support for the far right and far left in regional elections. 
 Merz’s conservatives won just 4.9 per cent of the vote in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party’s worst result in any state election in Germany’s postwar history. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) doubled its share of the vote and became the largest party in the former East German state. 
 The outcome means the CDU will fail to gain any seats in the regional parliament, according to preliminary results from state election authorities. ” 

 No seats? No problem… | Getty 
 Perusing the headlines in Germany’s neighbor to the west, where diesel prices hit an all-time record of $10.50 per gallon on Sunday, we learn that the political establishment is worried about developing unrest among the masses: 
 “ In France, concerns are mounting that the cost-of-living crisis may spiral into wider unrest. Fishermen blockaded several ports and a fuel depot along the Mediterranean coast in the past week. Meanwhile, calls are multiplying on social media to resume the Yellow-Vests protests, a grass-roots movement that started in 2018 and later morphed into nationwide riots. 
 French far-right leader and presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is among the politicians calling for a major cut in fuel taxes to deal with the crisis. ” 
 Here too, the country’s leader is setting records for unpopularity. President Emmanuel Macron’s approval rating has fallen to a low of 16% , levels that would have triggered an honor-salvaging resignation in prior times. Not so for Macron, who seems intent on riding things out until his term expires in 2027. 
 It is now certain that a full-blown and extended global diesel emergency is unavoidable, and the only questions remaining are those of degree and fallout. Unfortunately for the world, but especially for those living in Europe, we can think of four highly probable ways in which things are about to get even worse. In isolation or in normal times, each of these would constitute a serious development. Taken together and in the current context, this four-bet parlay of doom would usher in historically unprecedented levels of crisis. We might as well get ahead of things and prepare accordingly.
